doc.title: Peter Ecklund interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: The fragmented music business and looking back in pop
summary: He says it is a poor but interesting time to be a musician, and recounts touring with Madeleine Peyroux, noting pop musicians study the past.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Do you have any beefs with the music business these days that you run across in your particular field?

Well I suppose I should. I mean you get so used to taking things as they are and trying to find a way to take advantage of them. But that sort of discourages — I mean it’s easier to have beefs if you have some other means of support.

But we’re in kind of an interesting time now I think because I mean when I was younger, rock was sort of the all-encompassing — it was the only music that a lot of people my age thought should ever exist or —

Or did, yes. But now I think it’s getting kind of played out so it’s actually more interesting in general in the music business now that it’s so fragmented and that there’s so many styles. I mean there’s always a lot of mediocrity, and there’s certainly plenty of mediocrity now, but there’s no like one thing that has everyone’s imagination. So I think although the business, it’s not a very good time to be a musician, it’s sort of an interesting time to be around music.
Well there’s certainly a lot of styles: Cajun music and things that are kind of surfacing.

Well there’s a lot of focus on the past just in general, in all kinds of music. I mean rock music now, pop music, I just did a tour with the singer Madeleine Peyroux, and opening for Sarah McLachlan who’s like a pop singer, and I got to know the musicians and the music, and I’ve kind of been away from that scene for a while. And it’s like musicians who play pop music basically study everything that’s happened in the past thirty or forty years and kind of synthesize things, sort of the way I’ve done with traditional jazz. It’s not like everybody’s rushing out to buy the latest album by so-and-so, to find out what the new things are to do, because there really aren’t any. There are just kind of new instruments and new ways of mixing old stuff together. And that seems to be true across the board in most kinds of music and some of the more interesting music that’s happening now I think is mixtures of things that have been around for a while. And I think in music that’s generally the way things are. But it’s like since we have this — I guess maybe since the turn of the century music is kind of a generational thing.
